fact_claims.verbatim: 8.1 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units company-wide
four thermal incidents were not reported to a regulator
The Ember 8 had a 3.9% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test
81% of our installed units support remote emergency shut-off

behaviours.excerpt: These figures indicate the draft’s 8/100,000 recall trigger would apply to Northwind company-wide, though the Hearth 10’s model-specific rate is below that trigger.
behaviours.comparison: The S5 trigger in the draft is per model ("when a model’s annual thermal-incident rate exceeds 8 per 100,000"); Northwind's company-wide 8.6 does not by itself trigger a recall, so the claim misstates what the rule implies for Northwind.

fact_claims.verbatim: 8.6 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units company-wide
including 3 incidents not reported to a regulator
the Hearth 10 had a 6.2% failure rate in the 55 °C sustained-heat test
38% of Northwind’s installed units support remote emergency shut-off

S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report any battery thermal incident involving fire, smoke, uncontrolled overheating, evacuation, injury, or property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a full incident report within 10 calendar days. They must notify the affected household within 24 hours when safe contact details are available, and promptly notify nearby residents when the incident presents an ongoing hazard to them.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: A failure rate above 5% requires prompt notice to the regulator, a corrective-action plan, and confirmatory testing on a regulator-approved schedule. A model may remain on sale while following that plan unless the regulator determines a restriction is necessary based on the evidence and safety risk. A failure rate above 7% requires a regulator-directed risk assessment and may warrant a stop-sale or other protective measures.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: Newly installed systems must support remote emergency shut-off. Existing installed systems lacking this capability must be retrofitted or replaced within six years of the standard’s effective date, where technically feasible; the manufacturer must notify affected owners of the schedule and any interim safety measures.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: New home battery systems manufactured for sale must include built-in fire suppression meeting a regulator-approved performance and reliability standard. This requirement takes effect 36 months after adoption of the standard. Regulators may approve equivalent protective technology where it provides comparable fire-risk mitigation.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: If any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must notify the regulator and affected customers and initiate a recall with an effective remedy, such as repair, replacement, or refund, subject to regulator oversight. A recall requires an effective remedy; it does not by itself impose a market ban, though regulators may order a stop-sale or other measures when necessary to protect safety.

document.section_notes: S2 has no permanent numeric sales limit: the 5% and 7% figures trigger corrective action and risk assessment, and a stop-sale is discretionary, so a model like the Hearth 10 (6.2%) can keep selling. S5 keeps a mandatory recall at 8 per 100,000 with no transition period, which would apply to Halcyon's Ember 8 (9.9), though it expressly is not a market ban. S3 and S4 sit inside the acceptable bands (six-year retrofit with a feasibility qualifier, 36-month suppression requirement with equivalents allowed).
